title: Model Evaluation
summary: Calculate and interpret accuracy, precision, recall and a confusion matrix for a classification model.
objectives: Count true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives from predictions and true labels
Compute accuracy, precision and recall from those four counts
Explain why a high accuracy can hide a model that fails at its real job
Write a verdict on whether a model is useful for its stated purpose

segments.title: What you will build
segments.body:
## What you will build

A small company has built a spam filter, and on paper it looks good: 85% of its guesses are right. But the company has one rule: a filter is only useful if it catches at least 8 out of every 10 spam emails. In this lab you will read a file of 40 emails with the true label and the model's prediction, count the four kinds of outcome (TP, FP, FN, TN), and compute accuracy, precision and recall. Then you will write a one-sentence verdict that says whether the filter is good enough for its job, and why. This is the lesson from class: accuracy alone can hide a model that fails at the very thing it was built for.

segments.title: Lab: is the spam filter good enough?

lab.title: Is the spam filter good enough?
lab.objective: Compute a confusion matrix, precision and recall for a spam filter and give a verdict on whether it does its job.
lab.instructions:
The file predictions.csv has 40 rows and three columns: email_id, true_label and predicted_label. The labels are the words spam and not spam. Treat spam as the positive class.

1. Load the file with pandas: df = pd.read_csv("predictions.csv").
2. Count the four outcomes and store them in tp, fp, fn and tn:
   - tp: true label spam, predicted spam
   - fp: true label not spam, predicted spam
   - fn: true label spam, predicted not spam
   - tn: true label not spam, predicted not spam
   Loop over the rows with zip(df["true_label"], df["predicted_label"]), or use sklearn.metrics.confusion_matrix if you prefer.
3. Compute accuracy = (tp + tn) / 40, precision = tp / (tp + fp) and recall = tp / (tp + fn). Keep the full values in the variables; round only when printing.
4. Print seven lines in this order, rates rounded to 2 decimals:
TP: <count>
FP: <count>
FN: <count>
TN: <count>
Accuracy: <rate>
Precision: <rate>
Recall: <rate>
5. The company rule: the filter is good enough only if recall is at least 0.8. Set verdict to ONE sentence that starts with the exact words good enough or not good enough, then gives the reason and names recall. Print it as the last line: Verdict: <verdict>
lab.constraints: Read the labels from predictions.csv; do not type them into your code. Keep the names df, tp, fp, fn, tn, accuracy, precision, recall and verdict. Count every row: the four counts must add up to 40. No input().

lab.solution:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("predictions.csv")

tp = 0
fp = 0
fn = 0
tn = 0
for actual, predicted in zip(df["true_label"], df["predicted_label"]):
    if actual == "spam" and predicted == "spam":
        tp += 1
    elif actual == "not spam" and predicted == "spam":
        fp += 1
    elif actual == "spam" and predicted == "not spam":
        fn += 1
    else:
        tn += 1

accuracy = (tp + tn) / (tp + fp + fn + tn)
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
recall = tp / (tp + fn)

print("TP:", tp)
print("FP:", fp)
print("FN:", fn)
print("TN:", tn)
print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}")
print(f"Precision: {precision:.2f}")
print(f"Recall: {recall:.2f}")

if recall >= 0.8:
    verdict = f"good enough - recall is {recall:.2f}, so the filter catches most of the real spam"
else:
    verdict = f"not good enough - recall is only {recall:.2f}, so the filter misses most of the real spam even though accuracy looks high"
print("Verdict:", verdict)
